feedback: If a learner says 'that's a corner, not an angle' or 'a door opening isn't an angle', lay the different situations side by side and strip each to a vertex and two arms, naming the shared structure they all have.
If a learner only accepts an angle drawn upright, rotate the examples off the upright and confirm the vertex and arms are still there.
If a learner cannot find the ramp's angle, point out that only the slope line is drawn and draw in the horizontal arm with them so both arms are visible.
Praise locating the vertex correctly and reducing a real object to the two-ray diagram, not just naming the object.
activities.intendedInsight: A door, a clock and a pair of scissors are all the same underlying thing — two arms meeting at a point — so an angle is that shared skeleton, not any one particular picture. Some situations (slopes, sightings) have one arm that must be drawn in.
learnerActions: Gather or look at pictures of angles in many different situations: an open door, clock hands, open scissors, a propped ramp, a bent straw, a bend in a road, and the corner of a shape.
For each one, mark where the two arms are and put a dot on the vertex (the meeting point), drawing an arc at the vertex to show the angle.
Strip each situation down to the SAME bare diagram — two rays meeting at a point with an arc — and lay these stripped diagrams side by side.
Say in your own words what the door, the clock and the scissors all share.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit second arm (the horizontal ground line) so the angle has both arms.
activities.title: From many situations to one skeleton

feedback: If a learner predicts 'it gets bigger' when arms are lengthened, show the extended arms lying along the same two lines — it is the same angle — and return to the opening as the measure of size. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
If a learner cites arm length or the distance between arm-ends when comparing, extend a ray to show the angle is unchanged, and redirect attention to the opening/turn.
Affirm reasoning that refers to the opening or turn between the arms rather than to arm length.
activities.intendedInsight: The arms of an angle are rays that can be extended without changing the angle; the size is the opening (the turn) between the arms, not how long the arms are or how far apart the arm-ends sit.
learnerActions: Draw an angle, then predict (before doing anything) what will happen to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and say why.
Now extend both arms — or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, with the vertices aligned — and compare.
Describe what you notice: the longer arms lie along the same two lines, so the opening is unchanged.
Compare two angles that have the same opening but different arm lengths and decide whether they are equal, giving your reason.
activities.title: The arms are rays: lengthening does not change the angle

feedback: If a learner treats the corner and the turn as unrelated, slow down the opening of the hinge so they can see the same two arms both at rest and sweeping.
If a learner struggles to find the vertex on the clock, point to the centre where both hands begin and confirm the hands are the two arms.
Encourage describing the clock angle as the turn between the hands, linking it back to the corner view.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle has two connected conceptions — a static corner (two arms at a vertex) and a dynamic turn (an amount of rotation) — and these describe the same geometric object.
learnerActions: Take one object, such as an open door or a pair of scissors, and look at it as a static corner: two lines meeting at a point.
Now open and close it, watching the arms sweep through a turn, and notice the amount of turn is the size of the angle.
Explain how the still corner and the turning action describe the same angle on the same object.
Use a clock face: point to the vertex (the centre) and name the two hands as the two arms, then describe the angle as the turn between them.
activities.title: Connecting the corner and the turn

feedback: If a learner misses the rotated angle, rotate it back to upright, confirm it is an angle, then rotate it again so they see the angle is unchanged by orientation.
If a learner denies the ramp has an angle because only one line is drawn, draw in the horizontal arm with them.
If a learner claims the parallel lines make an angle, trace both lines and show they never meet, so there is no vertex.
Confirm a full explanation that names two rays, a shared vertex, and the opening/turn between them.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is two rays meeting at a vertex, recognisable even when rotated or when one arm is implicit; two lines that never meet do not form an angle because there is no shared vertex.
learnerActions: Look at a set of pictures: a clearly drawn angle, an angle rotated off the upright, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and two parallel lines that never meet.
For each picture, decide whether there is an angle and, if so, mark the vertex.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit horizontal arm and decide whether there is an angle there.
Say why the parallel lines do NOT form an angle (they never meet, so there is no vertex).
Explain in your own words what makes something an angle.
activities.title: Is it an angle? Including rotated and implicit-arm cases
